title: Philosophy: Big Ideas · Episode 3
chapters: Descartes: I think, therefore I am
Hume's problem: why trust that the sun will rise

units.t: Philosophy: Big Ideas. Episode three.
In this episode: Descartes: I think, therefore I am, The Enlightenment and Hume's problem: why trust that the sun will rise.
Part one. Descartes: I think, therefore I am.
What if everything you believe is a dream, or a trick?
René Descartes set out to doubt everything he possibly could, and what was left became one of the most famous sentences ever written.
Doubting everything.
In the winter of 1619, a young Frenchman named René Descartes was stuck in Germany, serving with an army.
By his own account, he spent a day alone in a stove-heated room, thinking.
Despite an excellent education, he felt much of what he had learned was uncertain.
Admiring the step-by-step certainty of geometry, he resolved to clear away every belief that could be doubted and see what solid ground remained.
In his Meditations of 1641 he began with the senses.
A tower looks round from far away and square up close; a straight stick looks bent in water.
A source that has fooled you once is not safe to trust fully.
This was a tool for one quiet hour of reflection, not a way to live as a sceptic.
The dream and the demon.
Descartes then raised a stronger worry.
He had often dreamed he was sitting by the fire in his dressing gown when he was actually asleep in bed.
Is there any sure sign that separates waking life from a vivid dream?
If not, even the scene in front of him might be unreal.
Finally he imagined an evil demon, supremely powerful and cunning, devoting all its energy to deceiving him about everything, perhaps even simple sums.
Modern philosophers have updated the demon into a brain in a vat, fed false experiences by scientists, an idea that inspired films such as The Matrix.
The question is the same: can you prove this is not happening to you right now?
The one certainty.
Here Descartes found his foothold.
Suppose the demon deceives him about everything.
Still, to be deceived, he must exist.
To doubt, he must be thinking.
However far the doubt is pushed, it cannot reach the fact that there is a doubter.
In the Meditations he put it as 'I am, I exist', which must be true whenever he thinks it.
In his earlier Discourse on the Method of 1637, written in French, he used the form that became famous, usually rendered in Latin as cogito, ergo sum: I think, therefore I am.
The early Christian thinker Augustine had made a similar point more than a thousand years earlier, arguing that if he was mistaken, he must exist to be mistaken.
Rebuilding, and mind and body.
Knowing only that you exist is a lonely position.
Descartes argued that his idea of a perfect being could only come from a perfect God, who would not deceive him, so clear and distinct perceptions could be trusted.
Critics noted the Cartesian circle: he seems to use clear ideas to prove God, then God to guarantee clear ideas.
His method also led to dualism.
He could doubt having a body but not that he was thinking, so mind must be a different kind of thing from body.
From 1643 Princess Elisabeth of Bohemia pressed him: if the mind is not physical, how can it move an arm?
He suggested the pineal gland in the brain, an answer few found satisfying.
Most philosophers and scientists today reject his dualism.
Why he still matters.
Descartes died in Stockholm in 1650, not long after moving there at the invitation of Queen Christina of Sweden.
By starting from the individual mind and asking what it can know for certain, he put epistemology, the study of knowledge, at the centre of philosophy for centuries.
Later thinkers such as John Locke and David Hume answered him by stressing experience over pure reason.
He also helped shape modern science and gave us coordinate geometry, the familiar x and y axes, called Cartesian coordinates.
Even people who reject his conclusions use his method: when in doubt, slow down, question your assumptions and ask what you really have good reason to believe.
The key idea: Descartes set out to clear away every doubtful belief and rebuild knowledge on a foundation that could not be doubted.
Part two. The Enlightenment.
In the 1700s, thinkers argued that reason, not tradition or kings, should guide human life.
Their ideas built the modern world.
Dare to know.
In 1784 the German philosopher Immanuel Kant answered the question 'What is Enlightenment?'
with a motto borrowed from the Roman poet Horace: sapere aude, 'dare to know'.
He meant having the courage to use your own understanding without being guided by someone else.

Building on the Scientific Revolution, thinkers across Europe and its colonies argued that reason and evidence, not tradition or superstition, should guide how we understand the world and organise society.
Isaac Newton's Principia, 1687, showed a few laws explaining both falling apples and orbiting planets.
If nature followed rational laws, why not society too?
The movement is usually dated from the late 1600s to around 1800.
Spreading the ideas.
Ideas spread through coffee houses, scientific societies, Parisian salons often hosted by women, and a booming trade in books.
The great project was the Encyclopédie, edited by Denis Diderot and Jean le Rond d'Alembert and published from 1751.
It aimed to gather all human knowledge, including practical trades, and French authorities repeatedly banned it.
Voltaire used wit and satire to attack intolerance and censorship.
His novel Candide, 1759, mocks blind optimism.
Jailed in the Bastille and later exiled, he campaigned to clear Jean Calas, a Protestant wrongly executed in 1762, and won in 1765.
The famous line 'I disapprove of what you say, but I will defend to the death your right to say it' wasn't his.
His biographer Evelyn Beatrice Hall wrote it in 1906.
Rights and consent.
The English philosopher John Locke, 1632 to 1704, argued that people are born with natural rights, including life, liberty and property, and that governments exist to protect them.
Government rests on the consent of the governed.
If it violates those rights, people may replace it.
In his Essay Concerning Human Understanding, 1689, he argued that the mind at birth is like a blank slate, shaped by experience rather than inborn ideas.
He also made an influential case for religious toleration.
His ideas deeply influenced the American Declaration of Independence, with its 'life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness', and later democratic constitutions.
Dividing power.
In The Spirit of the Laws, 1748, Montesquieu argued liberty is safest when power is divided: one body makes laws, another carries them out, and an independent judiciary interprets them.
Each checks the others, so no one becomes all-powerful.
This separation of powers became central to the US Constitution.
Australia's Constitution also separates legislative, executive and judicial power, and the High Court guarded judicial independence in the 1956 Boilermakers' case.
Jean-Jacques Rousseau opened The Social Contract, 1762, with: 'Man is born free, and everywhere he is in chains.'
He argued legitimate authority comes from the collective will of the people, not kings or force.
Critics note his claim that dissenters can be 'forced to be free' could justify authoritarianism.
Mary Wollstonecraft's Vindication of the Rights of Woman, 1792, extended these arguments to women.
Science, legacy, blind spots.
The Scottish Enlightenment produced David Hume, Adam Smith, The Wealth of Nations, 1776, and James Hutton, who argued the Earth was far older than most believed.
Enlightenment science reached Australia too: James Cook's voyage, backed by the Royal Society, observed the 1769 transit of Venus from Tahiti, then charted the east coast in 1770.
Joseph Banks collected thousands of plant specimens.
Free speech, tolerance, democracy and equal rights are Enlightenment legacies, running through the 1948 Universal Declaration of Human Rights.
But many thinkers accepted slavery, colonialism or the exclusion of women.
British colonisation of Australia began in 1788, with devastating effects on Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples.
Many argue the answer is to apply Enlightenment principles more consistently, not abandon them.
The key idea: The Enlightenment championed reason, evidence and individual rights over tradition and unquestioned authority.
Part three. Hume's problem: why trust that the sun will rise.
You are sure the sun will rise tomorrow.
But can you prove it?
David Hume's simple question about learning from experience has troubled philosophers and scientists for nearly three centuries, and a black swan from Western Australia became its mascot.
The question nobody asked.
In 1739 a young Scottish philosopher, David Hume, published A Treatise of Human Nature, which he later said 'fell dead-born from the press'.
In it, and in a 1748 book, he asked a question that seems almost silly.
Why do we believe the sun will rise tomorrow?
Because it always has.
But we have only observed the past.
Our confidence rests on an assumption that nature will keep behaving as it has.
There are two kinds of reasoning.
In deduction, true premises guarantee the conclusion.
Induction moves from observed cases to rules or predictions, so the conclusion could still be false.
Science, medicine and crossing the road depend on it.
Hume did not say stop using it.
He asked whether we can justify it without assuming what we are trying to prove.
The circle.
Hume's argument runs roughly like this.
A justification for induction must be either a deductive proof or an argument from experience.
It cannot be deductive, because there is no contradiction in imagining the future being different: you can coherently picture the sun failing to rise, or bread ceasing to nourish.
So it must come from experience.
But that argument would be: induction has worked in the past, so it will work in the future.
That is itself inductive, so it assumes the very thing in question.
Hume concluded that our expectations come not from reason but from custom or habit.
After seeing one event follow another many times, the mind simply comes to expect it.
It is now called the problem of induction, and it remains famously unsolved.
Chickens and black swans.
Bertrand Russell gave a grim illustration in 1912.
A chicken is fed every day by the farmer and comes to expect food whenever he appears.
One day, the farmer wrings its neck instead.
Its past experience was real, but it misled the chicken completely.
A more cheerful example comes from Australia.
For centuries Europeans used 'black swan' for something impossible, because every swan they had seen was white.
In 1697 the Dutch explorer Willem de Vlamingh's expedition recorded black swans on a river in Western Australia, which they named the Swan River.
A rule supported by countless observations was overturned by one.
The black swan is now a common emblem of the limits of induction.
Popper and grue.
The philosopher Karl Popper, in work first published in 1934, agreed that induction cannot be justified but argued science does not need it.
Scientists do not prove theories by piling up confirming cases.
They propose bold conjectures and try to refute them.
One genuine black swan falsifies 'all swans are white', and that is deduction.
Surviving theories are simply the best we have so far.
Critics reply that we still rely on tested theories to predict the future, which brings induction back.
In 1955 Nelson Goodman defined 'grue' as green if first observed before some future date, and blue otherwise.
Every emerald observed so far is both green and grue, so the evidence seems to support opposite predictions.
We should project green, but why?
The hard part is knowing which patterns count.
Living with uncertainty.
Many responses to Hume have been tried.
Some use probability and Bayesian reasoning to show how evidence should raise or lower our confidence, though critics say these methods still need assumptions about the world.
Others take a pragmatic line: if any method can predict the future, induction will, so it is our best bet.
Some argue that demanding a non-circular justification is unreasonable, since the most basic forms of reasoning cannot all be proved without using themselves.
Immanuel Kant said that reading Hume woke him from his 'dogmatic slumber'.
Whatever view you take, Hume's lesson is practical: hold general beliefs with confidence proportional to the evidence, and stay open to the black swan.
The key idea: Hume asked what justifies our expectation that the future will resemble the past, a question about induction.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. What was Descartes trying to do with his method of doubt?
Answer. Clear away doubtful beliefs to find a certain foundation.
Question two. What did Kant mean by 'dare to know'?
Answer. Using your own understanding with courage.
Question three. What is the problem of induction?
Answer. Our trust in the future rests on assuming nature stays as it was.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
